analogy.p: A resistor is a toll gate that always charges the same rate: twice the pressure, twice the traffic. A filament lamp is a road that narrows as traffic increases, because the busier it gets the hotter and more crowded it becomes. A diode is a one-way gate that opens only when pushed hard enough from the right side. The analogy breaks down because a real gate has a sharp opening, whereas the diode threshold is a smooth steep rise, and electrons are not separate vehicles.
analogy.t: Roads with different kinds of barrier

bullets: Know the **circuit**: component in series with an ammeter and variable resistor, voltmeter in parallel with the component.
Draw and recognise the **I-V graph of a resistor, a filament lamp and a diode**.
Explain each shape using **resistance** and, for the lamp, **temperature**.
State that the current in a **diode** flows in **one direction only**.
Calculate **resistance at a point** using R = V / I.
Evaluate the practical: variables, safety, sources of error.
AQA convention: **current on the y-axis, p.d. on the x-axis**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: You must be able to describe and carry out the required practical that produces **I-V characteristics** for a **fixed resistor**, a **filament lamp** and a **diode**, and then explain the shape of each graph in terms of resistance. The specification says that the current through an ohmic conductor (at constant temperature) is directly proportional to the p.d., that the resistance of a filament lamp increases as its temperature increases, and that the current through a diode flows in one direction only, with a very high resistance in the reverse direction. You must also be able to use the graphs to work out resistance.

bullets: **V = I R**, rearranged: **I = V / R** and **R = V / I**.
Units: **volt (V), ampere (A), ohm**; convert **mA to A** by dividing by 1000 (20 mA = 0.020 A).
Resistance depends on the component and, for the lamp, on its **temperature**.
For an ohmic conductor, **doubling the p.d. doubles the current** (directly proportional).
A steeper straight-line I-V graph means a **lower resistance** because the gradient is 1 / R.
For a curve, work out **R = V / I at one chosen point**, then repeat at another point to compare.
A larger resistance means **less current for the same p.d.**.
core.h: Resistance, V = IR and ohmic behaviour
core.p: Resistance is a measure of how hard it is for charge to flow through a component, and for any component it is defined by the equation **potential difference = current x resistance (V = I R)**, so **R = V / I**. The unit of p.d. is the volt (V), of current the ampere (A) and of resistance the ohm. For an **ohmic conductor at constant temperature** the resistance does not change, which is why current is directly proportional to p.d. and the graph is a straight line through the origin. A component whose resistance changes with p.d. or temperature is non-ohmic, and its resistance must be calculated separately at each point on its graph.

bullets: Apparatus: **cell or low-voltage power supply, variable resistor, ammeter, voltmeter, switch, leads** and the component under test.
The **component** (resistor, filament lamp or diode) is the thing whose I-V characteristic is being investigated.
The **variable resistor** is the way of changing the p.d. across the component.
The **ammeter** is in **series**; the **voltmeter** is in **parallel** across the component only.
For the **diode**, include a **protective resistor** in series to limit the current so the diode is not damaged.
A **reversing switch** or swapping the connections at the cell lets you collect **negative** values of V and I.
Use a **low p.d.** supply so that the equipment is safe and does not overheat.
core.h: The required practical: circuit and apparatus
core.p: To find how current varies with p.d. for a component, you need a circuit in which you can change the p.d. across the component and measure both quantities at the same time. A **variable resistor** in series with the component changes the current and hence the p.d. across the component. The **ammeter is connected in series** so that the same current flows through it as through the component, and the **voltmeter is connected in parallel** across the component only, so that it measures the p.d. across that component.

bullets: Set up the circuit with the first component and check the meters read zero when the circuit is off.
Close the switch and adjust the variable resistor to give the **smallest p.d.**; record **V and I**.
Move the variable resistor in steps to increase the p.d.; record **V and I** at each step (at least 8 to 10 sets).
Open the switch between readings if the component warms up, so it can cool.
**Reverse the connections** to the cell (or use a reversing switch) and repeat to record **negative p.d. and current**.
Repeat with the other components, using the **same method**.
**Plot I against V** for each, with a smooth line or curve of best fit, and describe the shape.
core.h: The required practical: method step by step
core.p: The method is the same for all three components: set the variable resistor, record the ammeter and voltmeter readings, then change the setting and repeat. The independent variable is the p.d. across the component and the dependent variable is the current through it. After a set of readings in one direction, reverse the connections to the supply and repeat so that you can plot the full graph with negative values. Then replace the component and repeat.

bullets: **Independent variable**: p.d. across the component (V).
**Dependent variable**: current through the component (A).
**Control variables**: the same component, and for the resistor, **constant temperature** (low currents, switched off between readings).
Do not exceed the **rated voltage** of the lamp or the **current rating** of the diode.
A hot lamp can cause **burns**: do not touch it during or just after the experiment.
Take **more readings** around the region where the graph is changing quickly (for example near the diode threshold).
Use meters with a **suitable range and resolution**, and check for **zero errors**.
core.p: The independent variable is the **potential difference across the component** and the dependent variable is the **current through it**. The control variables are the component itself and, as far as possible, its **temperature**. Because the filament lamp changes temperature as current flows, its temperature cannot be kept constant, which is exactly why its resistance changes. A good evaluation discusses the range and number of readings and how to improve accuracy.

bullets: Shape: **straight line through the origin**, extending into the negative quadrants.
**I is directly proportional to V**; doubling V doubles I.
**Resistance is constant**: R = V / I has the same value at every point.
On an I-V graph the **gradient = 1 / R**; a steeper line means a **lower resistance**.
The resistor behaves the same in **both directions** of current.
This is an **ohmic conductor** (provided the temperature is constant).
If the resistor overheats, the line would start to bend and it would no longer be ohmic.
core.h: The fixed resistor: a straight line through the origin
core.p: For a fixed resistor at constant temperature the I-V graph is a **straight line through the origin**. This shows that current is **directly proportional** to p.d., so the resistance (V / I) is the same at every point. The line is the same in the negative quadrant, so the resistor behaves the same whichever way the current flows. A steeper line means a smaller resistance, because the same p.d. produces a larger current.

bullets: Shape: **curve that flattens** as V increases; passes through the origin; symmetrical.
As V rises, I rises but **by less and less**; the lamp is **non-ohmic**.
Explanation: **higher current = higher temperature of the filament = greater resistance**.
The metal ions vibrate more, so the **electrons collide with the ions more often**.
Resistance at any point is **R = V / I**; it **increases** as the point moves along the curve.
The filament may reach a very high temperature (it glows white), so resistance when on is much larger than when cold.
Use the phrase **'resistance increases as the temperature increases'**, which is the wording in the specification.
core.h: The filament lamp: resistance increases with temperature
core.p: The I-V graph for a filament lamp is an **S-shaped curve** through the origin, symmetrical in the positive and negative quadrants. At first the graph is nearly straight, but as the p.d. rises the line gets **less steep**. The current is no longer proportional to the p.d. The explanation is that as current flows the filament **heats up**; the ions in the metal vibrate with greater amplitude, so electrons collide with them **more frequently**, and the **resistance increases**.

bullets: Shape: flat along the x-axis in reverse, near zero current, then a **sharp rise** in the forward direction after the threshold.
**Forward direction**: low resistance once above the threshold p.d.; the current rises steeply.
**Reverse direction**: very high resistance, so virtually **no current**.
The diode is **non-ohmic**: current is not proportional to p.d.
A **light-emitting diode (LED)** emits light when current flows in the forward direction.
Diodes are used to make sure current flows the **right way round**, and in rectifying a.c. to d.c.
A **protective resistor** is needed in the circuit so the forward current does not become too large.
core.h: The diode: current in one direction only
core.p: A **diode** is a component that allows current to flow through it in **one direction only**. Its I-V graph shows that in the **forward direction** there is almost no current until the p.d. reaches a **threshold value** (about 0.6 to 0.7 V for a typical silicon diode), after which the current rises very **steeply**. In the **reverse direction** the current is almost zero for any p.d. This means the resistance is **very high in the reverse direction**, and low in the forward direction above the threshold.

bullets: Pick the **point** on the curve and read **V and I** from the axes.
**R = V / I** at that point (not the slope of the curve).
For the **filament lamp**, R at higher V is **larger** than R at lower V.
For the **resistor**, R is the **same** at every point, so you can use any pair of values.
For the **diode**, R in the reverse direction is **very large**, and in the forward direction above threshold R is **small**.
Convert **mA to A** before calculating.
Quote the answer in **ohm** with the right number of significant figures.
core.h: Calculating resistance from an I-V graph
core.p: For a straight-line graph through the origin the resistance is constant, but for a curve you must find the resistance **at a particular point** by reading the values of V and I at that point and using **R = V / I**. Do not use the gradient of the tangent for this, because on an I-V graph the gradient equals 1 / R only for a straight line through the origin. Reading carefully from the grid, taking the correct units, and converting mA to A are the key skills.

bullets: **Resistor**: straight line through origin; **constant** resistance; symmetrical.
**Filament lamp**: S-curve; resistance **increases** with temperature; symmetrical.
**Diode**: zero current in reverse; steep rise after threshold in forward; **not symmetrical**.
Only the **resistor** is ohmic.
The filament lamp and the diode are **non-ohmic**.
Symmetry test: if the graph in the negative quadrants is a **mirror through the origin** of the positive part, the component works the same in both directions.
If current barely changes as V increases, the **resistance is very high**.
core.p: Examiners often ask you to compare graphs or identify a component from its graph. The key is to look at the shape and symmetry, and then explain with resistance. A straight line through the origin means a constant resistance; a curve that flattens means a rising resistance; a graph that is flat in reverse and then steep in forward means a diode. Each graph can be linked directly to a physical explanation.

bullets: Chain for the lamp: **current -> heating -> ions vibrate more -> more frequent collisions -> higher resistance -> less steep graph**.
Mention **temperature** explicitly; the lamp is the component whose temperature changes noticeably.
The resistor is straight only if its **temperature is constant**.
For the diode, the explanation is a property of the component: it allows current in **one direction only**.
Always use the words **'resistance increases'** or **'resistance is very high'**, not 'harder for electricity to flow'.
Link the graph to **R = V / I**: if I rises less than V, then V / I rises.
core.p: 'Why is the graph curved?' is a common question, and the reasoning has a chain of steps that gains full marks. For the lamp the chain is: current flows, so the filament heats; the ions vibrate more; more frequent collisions with electrons; resistance increases; so the current increases by less for each extra volt. A single statement such as 'because the resistance changes' is not enough without the cause.

bullets: Axes: **current (A)** on the y-axis, **p.d. (V)** on the x-axis, both labelled with units.
Choose **scales** that use at least half the grid, with equal steps.
Plot points as small crosses and draw a **smooth curve or straight line of best fit**.
Draw a **ruler line** for the resistor; a **smooth curve** for the lamp and diode.
Include the **negative** quadrants if reverse readings were taken.
**Anomalies**: a point far from the line should be repeated; do not force the curve through it.
Describe a graph using a **pattern + data**: 'as V increases from 0 to 6 V, current increases from 0 to 0.8 A, but by smaller amounts each time.'
core.p: In the exam you may be given a table of readings and asked to plot an I-V graph or to describe a graph. Use sensible scales so that the plotted points fill more than half of the grid, label the axes with the quantity and the unit, plot carefully, and draw a smooth line through the points. If the readings for a diode are close together at the threshold, add more points there.

bullets: **Resistance and V = I R** (previous spec point).
**LDRs and thermistors** (next spec point) are also components whose resistance changes.
**Power**: P = I V and P = I squared x R show how much energy per second is transferred; the lamp's heating is why its resistance changes.
**Series and parallel circuits**: the p.d. is shared in series, the current is shared in parallel.
**Mains electricity**: a.c. has current changing direction; a diode can make the current flow only one way.
**Energy transfers**: electrical energy is transferred to thermal energy in the lamp filament.
**Higher tier extension**: use the graphs to find the p.d. across a component in a circuit when the current is known.
core.p: This spec point connects to many other parts of Physics. Thermistors and LDRs give I-V characteristics too, series and parallel rules build on the resistance idea, and power (P = I V) relates to the heating that changes the lamp's resistance. In industry, diodes protect circuits and LEDs light our homes.

bullets: Always use the three words **shape, resistance, reason** to structure an answer.
Say 'resistance **increases** as temperature increases' for the filament lamp, not just 'it gets harder'.
For the diode say it has a **very high resistance in the reverse direction**, so current flows **one direction only**.
Use **'p.d.' across a component and 'current through' it**, never the other way round.
Quote **data from the graph with units** when asked to calculate.
If a graph has negative values, state that the component is **tested in both directions**.
Check your answer is a sensible size: lamp resistance is a few ohms; diode forward current is mA.
core.h: Exam-style reasoning chain for each graph
core.p: A reliable way to earn full marks on any I-V question is to give a three-part answer: describe the shape, state what happens to the resistance, then give the physical reason. For the resistor the shape is a straight line through the origin, the resistance is constant, and the reason is that the temperature is constant so the charge carriers meet the same obstruction at every p.d. For the lamp the line curves so that the current rises by less and less, the resistance increases, and the reason is that the heated filament has ions vibrating more so electrons collide with them more often. For the diode there is no current until a threshold p.d. in the forward direction and almost none in reverse, so the resistance is low forward and very high in reverse.

exam: **Draw** the circuit (2 to 3 marks): cell, variable resistor and ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel across the component; use correct symbols.
**Describe** the shape of a graph (2 marks): give the shape and relate to the data, for example 'straight line through the origin'.
**Explain** the lamp curve (3 to 4 marks): current heats the filament; ions vibrate more; more collisions with electrons; resistance increases.
**Explain** the diode graph: current flows in one direction only; very high resistance in the reverse direction.
**Calculate** resistance at a point: write R = V / I, read values, substitute, give the unit.
**Identify** a component from its graph: straight line = resistor; S-curve = lamp; flat then steep = diode.
In a **6 mark** practical question include: circuit, variable resistor, readings of V and I, repeating with reversed connections, graph, safety.
Use the specification phrase '**resistance increases as the temperature increases**' for the lamp.
When asked to **compare** two graphs, write one point about each, linked with 'whereas'.
State **units** (A, V, ohm) in all answers and axis labels.

mistakes.r: The voltmeter must be in parallel across the component; the ammeter is in series.
mistakes.w: The voltmeter is connected in series.

mistakes.r: The curve flattens, so resistance increases with temperature; passing through the origin only shows I = 0 when V = 0.
mistakes.w: The lamp's resistance stays constant because the graph passes through the origin.

mistakes.r: A diode allows current in one direction only (the forward direction) and has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
mistakes.w: The diode does not allow any current at all.

mistakes.r: Resistance at a point = V / I at that point.
mistakes.w: Resistance on a curve is the gradient of the curve.

mistakes.r: It is curved because the resistance changes as the filament temperature rises.
mistakes.w: The graph is curved because the voltage changes.

mistakes.r: The ions vibrate with more energy so electrons collide with them more frequently, increasing resistance.
mistakes.w: The lamp gets hotter so the electrons move faster and meet ions.

mistakes.r: AQA convention: current on the y-axis and p.d. on the x-axis for I-V graphs.
mistakes.w: Axes swapped: p.d. on the y-axis.

mistakes.r: Reverse the connections and take readings for negative p.d. to complete the graph.
mistakes.w: Using the same component in reverse needs no new readings.

summary: You must be able to describe the required practical for I-V characteristics, draw and explain the graphs for a fixed resistor, filament lamp and diode, and calculate resistance at a point from a graph. It matters because it tests practical skills, graph interpretation and the idea that resistance can change.

terms.d: A graph of current (y-axis) against potential difference (x-axis) for a component.
A conductor for which current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature.
A component for which current is not proportional to p.d., such as a filament lamp or diode.
A lamp with a thin metal filament whose resistance increases as its temperature increases.
A component that allows current to flow in one direction only; it has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
The p.d. in the forward direction above which a diode conducts and the current rises steeply.
The direction in which a diode allows current to flow.
The direction in which a diode has a very high resistance and almost no current flows.
Light-emitting diode: a diode that emits light when current flows through it.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed to vary the current and the p.d. across the component.
A resistor in series that limits the current to prevent damage to a component such as a diode.
The ratio of two quantities is constant; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
The variable that you deliberately change (p.d. across the component).
The variable you measure (current through the component).
An error that shifts all readings the same way, such as zero error on a meter.
The opposition to current in a component, calculated as p.d. divided by current (R = V / I); unit: ohm.
Change in y divided by change in x; on an I-V graph a straight-line gradient equals 1 / R.

worked.ans: 5.0 ohm at 2.0 V; 8.0 ohm at 6.0 V; resistance increases because the filament gets hotter.
worked.q: The I-V graph for a filament lamp shows a current of 0.40 A at 2.0 V and 0.75 A at 6.0 V. Calculate the resistance of the lamp at each p.d. and explain the difference. (4 marks)
steps: The resistance is greater at the higher p.d.
Reason: the larger current heats the filament more, so ions vibrate more and electrons collide more frequently.

worked.q: A diode conducts a current of 20 mA when the forward p.d. across it is 0.80 V. Calculate its resistance in this direction. (3 marks)

worked.ans: A full-mark answer has the correct circuit, a way of varying p.d., readings of both V and I, reversing the connections, plotting I against V, and the safety point about not exceeding the rated voltage.
worked.q: Describe how you would obtain the I-V characteristic for a filament lamp. (6 marks)
steps: Build a series circuit with the cell, variable resistor, ammeter, switch and lamp.
Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the lamp only.
Use the variable resistor to set a small p.d.; record the voltmeter and ammeter readings.
Increase the p.d. in steps, recording V and I each time (about 8 to 10 readings), staying below the rated voltage.
Reverse the connections to the cell and repeat to collect negative values.
Plot I (y-axis) against V (x-axis) and draw a smooth curve; it is an S-shaped curve through the origin.
